analysis.one_liner: Makes national banks follow state consumer protection laws and lets state attorneys general enforce them.
analysis.headline: Six Democratic senators backed the bill, but it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in October 2004 and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overturned, by statute, federal rules that shield national banks from state consumer protection laws. It would make state consumer and fraud laws apply to national banks, restore state attorneys general's power to sue national banks and recover damages for their residents, and require the Comptroller of the Currency to track and publicly report consumer complaints against national banks. It was introduced in the last weeks of the 108th Congress and died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers, especially people in states with stronger consumer protection, lending, or fraud laws, who would gain enforceable rights against national banks and their subsidiaries; state attorneys general, who could again sue national banks and recover damages for state residents; and the public generally, through a public, semiannual record of consumer complaints against national banks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers and state attorneys general

how_it_helps.text: Any state consumer law of general application — including unfair-or-deceptive-practices laws and consumer fraud laws — would apply to national banks, closing the gap left by federal preemption rules.

State attorneys general could enforce federal and state laws against national banks and sue on behalf of residents to recover damages, powers the bill says federal visitorial-power rules cannot be read to limit.
State law would apply to state-chartered, nondepository subsidiaries of national banks (such as mortgage or lending units) unless Congress had explicitly preempted it.

The Comptroller of the Currency would have to record and monitor every consumer complaint about a national bank or its subsidiary, report semiannually to Congress on complaint volumes and resolution times, and post those reports publicly on its website.

analysis.who_pays: National banks and their nondepository subsidiaries, which would have to comply with the consumer laws of every state where they operate and defend suits by state attorneys general; some of that compliance cost could reach customers through higher fees or rates.

drawbacks.text: National banks operate in all 50 states, so applying each state's consumer and fraud laws to them creates a patchwork of differing rules; banks argued this raises compliance costs that can be passed to customers through higher fees or rates.

State-by-state enforcement would add a layer of litigation on top of the Comptroller of the Currency's federal supervision of national banks, which supporters of the 2004 preemption rules said could produce inconsistent or duplicative regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: enforceable state consumer protections and state attorneys general with standing to sue the largest banks, plus a public record of complaints the regulator must track and publish. The main cost is compliance complexity for banks that operate nationwide. The bill was written to blunt the strongest objection — it exempts state laws that discriminate against national banks and defers to explicit congressional preemption — so the tradeoff favors consumers, though the patchwork concern for multi-state lenders is genuine.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the final weeks of the 108th Congress and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Corzine introduced the bill on October 9, 2004, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Senators Boxer, Murray, Schumer, Lautenberg, and Leahy.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The action record shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National banks and the Comptroller of the Currency, who kept the 2004 federal preemption rules the bill targeted; state attorneys general and bank customers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it upon introduction; it was referred to committee the same day.

against.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
against.role: Chairman, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: National banking industry
against.what_they_did: Supported the federal preemption regime the bill sought to overturn and opposed restoring state authority over national banks.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all six sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Banking Committee, with a 55-seat Republican majority in the Senate, never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would strip away the federal preemption shields that exempt national banks from state consumer, lending, and fraud laws, and would let state attorneys general sue them for damages on behalf of customers. Banks would bear new compliance costs across 50 state regimes, while consumers would gain enforceable remedies.

industries.industry: Nondepository subsidiaries of national banks (mortgage and consumer lending units)
industries.note: The bill would make state law apply to these state-chartered subsidiaries unless Congress had explicitly preempted it, ending the practice of routing lending operations through nationally chartered entities to escape state rules.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and state governments
industries.note: The bill would restore their authority to enforce state and federal law against national banks and to recover damages for state residents, reversing the limits on state enforcement set by federal regulators.

industries.industry: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
industries.note: The bill would override the OCC's 2004 preemption determinations and add mandatory complaint tracking and semiannual public reporting, reducing its discretion as sole supervisor of national banks.
